source_row: HODGE-RG-002; gallery hard-excluded general fourfold codim-two
prompt: A draft caption says: 'This class in H^4(X,Q) cap H^{2,2}(X) is of type (2,2), which is exactly the condition for being the class of an algebraic cycle, so the cycle exists.' Is the caption right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
known_because: the general fourfold codimension-two case is the first open Hodge range; type (p,p) is the admissible shadow, not a construction
tempting_wrong_answer: The caption is right; rational type (2,2) is exactly the condition for being a cycle class, so the cycle exists.
correct_answer: No. Rational type (2,2) is the admissible shadow, not a construction: the reverse direction from shadow to cycle is the Hodge conjecture, open in exactly this range. Repair: 'a rational (2,2) class - the shadow an algebraic cycle would cast; whether a cycle exists here is the open question.' The slip is R3 presented as R4; the register audit's source-anchor check catches it.
register_changed: R3 (rational class) silently promoted to R4 (algebraic cycle)
repair: Label the class as the admissible shadow; state that shadow-to-body here is the open Hodge conjecture, not a generator rule.

prompt: A draft exhibit says: 'The curve's rich H^1 is where the geometry lives, so we use H^1 as the shadow whose hidden algebraic body the visitor must find.' Is this admissible? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
body: a point, for the admitted H^2 row
shadow: the generator of H^2(C,Q), of type (1,1)
known_because: H^1 of a curve decomposes as (1,0)+(0,1) and is not a (p,p) Hodge target; the admitted row is the point class in H^2
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; use the curve's rich H^1 as the hidden-body card because that is where the geometry lives.
correct_answer: No. H^1 is not a (p,p) target - it splits as (1,0)+(0,1) - so it cannot be the shadow of a Hodge-cycle card. The admitted row is the point class in H^2, a trivial known case. Repair: keep H^1 as background texture and run the card on H^2. The slip is roster admission (a non-(p,p) group cast as the shadow); the admission fence catches it.
register_changed: non-(p,p) cohomology admitted as an R3 shadow
repair: Run the card on the point class in H^2; keep H^1 as explicitly non-target background.

prompt: A draft caption says: 'Here a rational (1,1) class on a surface is realized by a curve - a new Hodge phenomenon beyond the divisor case.' Is the caption right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
body: a curve on the surface, i.e. a divisor
shadow: a rational (1,1) class in NS(S) tensor Q
known_because: a curve on a surface has codimension one; this is Lefschetz (1,1) again
tempting_wrong_answer: The caption is right; curves on a surface are a separate higher-codimension case beyond divisors.
correct_answer: No. A curve on a surface has codimension one - it is a divisor, so this is the Lefschetz (1,1) theorem in concrete clothing, not a new phenomenon. Repair: 'the divisor theorem, shown on a surface.' The slip is a known p=1 case dressed as higher codimension; the toy-laundering check catches it.
register_changed: known p=1 case re-labeled as a new higher-codimension phenomenon
repair: Re-caption as Lefschetz (1,1) specialized to surfaces; the codimension is one.

prompt: A draft caption says: 'On this threefold the rational (2,2) class is a curve class; the same therefore holds for every integral class in this range.' Is the upgrade right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
known_because: hard Lefschetz reduces codimension n-1 rational Hodge to codimension one; the integral variant is false in general (Atiyah-Hirzebruch type counterexamples)
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; if the rational class is algebraic, every integral class in the same range is algebraic too.
correct_answer: No. The row is rational only. The integral Hodge statement is a separate, false-in-general variant and must be labeled separately - the silent upgrade from rational to integral is exactly the trap. Repair: append 'rationally' and fence the integral case as known-false in general. The slip is the rational/integral fence; the lit-mismatch check catches it.
register_changed: rational statement silently upgraded to integral
repair: State the result with 'rationally'; label integral Hodge as a distinct false-in-general variant.

prompt: A draft page says: 'This compact Kaehler manifold has harmonic representatives and (p,p) classes, so the smooth-projective Hodge card applies unchanged.' Is the reuse right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
shadow: a (p,p) class outside the smooth-projective roster
known_because: the rational Hodge conjecture lane is smooth projective; Kaehler analogues fail and are hard-excluded by the reader fence
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; Hodge theory and harmonic representatives exist on Kaehler manifolds, so the same algebraic-cycle question applies unchanged.
correct_answer: No. The lane is smooth projective; compact Kaehler is not a safe substitute (Kaehler analogues of the conjecture fail), and the generator must not admit it. Repair: fence the page to smooth projective or re-label the Kaehler example as a hard-excluded boundary exhibit. The slip is the domain fence; the admission audit catches it.
register_changed: domain widened from smooth projective to compact Kaehler without re-fencing
repair: Restrict to smooth projective, or exhibit Kaehler as an explicitly excluded boundary row.

source_row: HODGE-RG-009; reader fence Hodge loci != cycle construction
prompt: A draft caption says: 'The locus where this class stays type (p,p) is algebraic - so the cycle behind the class has been found.' Is the inference right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
body: none licensed by locus algebraicity alone
shadow: a class whose (p,p) type persists on a locus
known_because: Cattani-Deligne-Kaplan gives algebraicity of Hodge loci, not construction of cycles
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; if the Hodge locus is algebraic, the cycle behind the class has been found.
correct_answer: No. Cattani-Deligne-Kaplan makes the shadow's stability locus algebraic; it constructs no cycle. A structured shadow-locus is not a body. Repair: 'the locus where the shadow persists is algebraic (CDK); whether a cycle casts it remains open.' The slip is shadow-stability presented as body-construction; the locus/cycle fence catches it.
repair: Attribute algebraicity to the locus via CDK and state the cycle question stays open.

prompt: A draft caption under a q=5 finite-field display says: 'Signature 10000 pins down the displayed point set - indeed, adding any single point would change the signature.' Is either claim right? If not, repair the caption, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
body: any of 105 point sets at q=5 (the q(q^2-q+1) law)
known_because: the audit enumerates 105 bodies casting 10000 at q=5; a line plus one off-line point casts the same signature (registered guard witness)
tempting_wrong_answer: Both claims are right; the signature identifies the set and adding a point changes the signature.
correct_answer: No, both claims fail. The signature is a lossy projection - 105 distinct bodies cast 10000 at q=5 - and adding one off-line point cannot complete a line in a new direction, so the signature does not change. Repair: 'one of q(q^2-q+1) bodies casting this signature; single points come and go invisibly.' The slip is body data read off the shadow; the shadow-reencoding guard catches it.
register_changed: body identity and body change both attributed to the shadow
repair: State the collision count q(q^2-q+1) and the line-plus-point guard witness; the shadow forgets points.

prompt: A draft caption says: 'This set has q(q+1)/2 points - the Dvir bound - so its direction coverage is complete.' Is the inference right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
body: a floor-size set can cluster and miss directions
shadow: the signature need not be complete
known_because: the Dvir floor is necessary for complete coverage, not sufficient
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; reaching the Dvir floor size forces complete direction coverage.
correct_answer: No. The Dvir floor is a lower bound for sets that already have complete coverage; it is not sufficient. A floor-size set can cluster and miss directions entirely. Repair: 'large enough to be Kakeya, but coverage must be verified separately.' The slip is a necessary bound read as sufficient; the size-overclaim check catches it.
register_changed: necessary size bound inverted into a sufficient coverage claim
repair: State the floor as necessary-only; verify coverage from the line table, not the count.

prompt: A draft metric panel says: 'The adaptive-over-fixed coverage gap on this dense body measures Kakeya body resistance.' Is the metric right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
body: none licensed by the raw gap
known_because: the H-K4 panel showed random same-size bodies reproduce the raw gap on dense bodies (finite-grid density artifact); signal survives only sparse, as excess over a size-matched control
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; the adaptive-over-fixed gap measures Kakeya body resistance.
correct_answer: No. On dense bodies the raw gap is a finite-grid density artifact - random same-size bodies reproduce it. A structure-driven reading survives only in the sparse regime and only as excess over a size-matched random control. Repair: report gap-minus-control, sparse regime only. The slip is an uncontrolled statistic presented as a metric; the density-artifact check (the panel's own falsifier) catches it.
register_changed: uncontrolled raw statistic promoted to a resistance metric
repair: Subtract the size-matched random control and restrict to the sparse regime before reporting.

source_row: KAK-RG-004; Euclidean boundary after Wang-Zahl in R^3
prompt: A draft page says: 'Between this finite-field workbench and the Wang-Zahl result in R^3, the Euclidean Kakeya problem is settled in all dimensions.' Is the claim right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
target_register: finite-field workbench vs Euclidean problem (domain fence)
shadow: finite-field collision counts and a dimension-specific Euclidean result
known_because: none - boundary card. Dvir's finite-field theorem is a different problem from Euclidean Kakeya; Wang-Zahl addresses R^3, and higher dimensions remain open.
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; the finite-field results plus Wang-Zahl in R^3 settle Euclidean Kakeya in all dimensions.
correct_answer: No, twice over. The finite-field workbench is a different problem from Euclidean Kakeya and settles nothing Euclidean; and Wang-Zahl concerns R^3 specifically - higher-dimensional Euclidean Kakeya remains open. Repair: fence the workbench as finite-field-only and cite Wang-Zahl as an R^3 result. The slip is a domain leap; the Euclidean-leap fence catches it.
register_changed: finite-field workbench and one R^3 theorem promoted to an all-dimensions Euclidean claim
repair: Fence the workbench to finite fields; state Wang-Zahl's scope as R^3 with higher dimensions open.

prompt: A draft synthesis says: 'The Kakeya collision count q(q^2-q+1) and the Hodge overclaim rate are the same invariant measured in two lanes - the shadow-collision table is an isomorphism.' Is that right? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
known_because: the HK5 table clears its falsifier as a calibrated analogy with a typed mismatch: Kakeya lossiness is a finite count, Hodge lossiness is a decoder rate
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; the count and the rate are the same invariant, and the table is an isomorphism between the lanes.
correct_answer: No. The table is a calibrated analogy, not an isomorphism: Kakeya's lossiness is a finite body-count per signature, Hodge's is a decoder overclaim rate - same frame and same non-invertibility idea, different units. Kakeya is finite resist (size pinned), Hodge infinite resist (existence undecidable). Repair: state the typed mismatch explicitly. The slip is analogy promoted to identity; the only-rhyme check catches it in reverse.
register_changed: calibrated analogy promoted to isomorphism (count conflated with rate)
repair: Keep the shared schema but state the count-vs-rate typed mismatch and the finite/infinite resist split.

source_row: H-K4 null + PHASE4F correction; control discipline
prompt: A draft results page reports a single collision statistic - 'many bodies share this shadow' - as self-evident proof of lossiness, with no baseline. Is the report right as it stands? If not, repair it, say which register slipped, and name the check that should have caught it.
known_because: both lanes' receipts show raw statistics over-credit: the Kakeya adaptive gap was a density artifact until compared to random same-size bodies, and the Hodge lexical route check over-credited until checked against independent semantic judges
tempting_wrong_answer: Yes; the collision statistic speaks for itself - many bodies sharing a shadow is proof enough.
correct_answer: No. Both lanes' receipts show raw statistics over-credit: the Kakeya gap was a finite-grid density artifact until measured against random same-size controls, and the Hodge lexical score over-credited until audited by independent judges. Repair: publish the statistic with its matched control (random baseline or independent judge) or not at all. The slip is measurement without control; the lane's own artifact checks catch it.
register_changed: uncontrolled statistic presented as self-evident measurement
repair: Pair every collision/lossiness number with its size-matched control or independent judge before reporting.
